tele-042.explication: ARTESiA enrolled about 4000 patients aged 55 years or over with a pacemaker, ICD or implantable monitor, subclinical AF lasting 6 minutes to 24 hours and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 3. Apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism by about 37% compared with aspirin (about 0.8% vs 1.2% per year), with a higher rate of major bleeding (about 1.7% vs 0.9% per year). The absolute stroke risk therefore remains low, well below that of clinical AF. The comparator was aspirin, not placebo, and the patients had subclinical AF, not clinical AF.
tele-042.aRetenir: ARTESiA: apixaban > aspirin for stroke in subclinical AF, but more bleeding and a low absolute risk.
tele-042.rappel: In subclinical AF, stroke risk is much lower than in clinical AF, around 1% per year or slightly more. With such a low baseline risk, even a large relative reduction in stroke with a DOAC translates into a modest absolute benefit, which must be weighed against the absolute increase in major bleeding. This is why interpretation of an anticoagulation trial must always distinguish relative from absolute effect and take the comparator (aspirin or placebo) into account.

tele-043.question: What was the main result of the NOAH-AFNET 6 trial (Kirchhof, NEJM 2023) in patients with atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE)?
options: Edoxaban superior to placebo for stroke, at the cost of more bleeding
Early termination, no significant reduction in events, more bleeding
Stroke rate of about 5% per year on placebo, justifying anticoagulation
Halving of all-cause mortality on edoxaban, with no excess bleeding
commentaires: Incorrect: edoxaban did not significantly reduce the efficacy endpoint.
Correct: stopped for futility and a safety signal; the composite of death or major bleeding was increased.
Incorrect: the stroke rate on placebo was low, about 1% per year.
Incorrect: no mortality benefit, and bleeding was more frequent.
tele-043.explication: NOAH-AFNET 6 randomised about 2500 patients aged 65 years or over, with at least one risk factor and AHREs lasting at least 6 minutes, to edoxaban or placebo. The trial was stopped early for futility and because of a safety signal. Edoxaban did not significantly reduce the efficacy endpoint and increased the composite of death or major bleeding. The stroke rate on placebo was low (about 1% per year), well below that of clinical AF. This result, which contrasts with ARTESiA, explains the cautious recommendation (class IIb) in the 2024 ESC guidelines.
tele-043.aRetenir: NOAH-AFNET 6: no significant benefit of edoxaban for AHREs, more bleeding, strokes rare.
tele-043.rappel: AHREs detected by implanted devices correspond to AF episodes that are often short and of low burden, with a low thromboembolic risk, around 1% per year without anticoagulation. In such a low-risk population, the absolute benefit of an anticoagulant is small, whereas the bleeding risk remains that of anticoagulation. A trial may also be stopped early for futility (an effect is unlikely) or because of a safety signal. These data, which are inconsistent across trials, explain why anticoagulation for subclinical AF is an individualised decision.

tele-044.question: The meta-analysis of NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESiA (McIntyre, Circulation 2024) showed that, in device-detected AF, DOACs:
options: Reduce all-cause mortality by a third, at the cost of more bleeding
Have no effect on ischaemic stroke but increase major bleeding
Reduce ischaemic stroke by a third, more bleeding, mortality unchanged
Reduce ischaemic stroke and, paradoxically, major bleeding
commentaires: Incorrect: the meta-analysis showed no difference in cardiovascular or all-cause mortality.
Incorrect: this is the conclusion one would draw from NOAH-AFNET 6 alone; pooled, the trials show about 32% fewer ischaemic strokes.
Correct: RR for ischaemic stroke around 0.68, major bleeding increased by about 60%, mortality unchanged.
Incorrect: major bleeding increased by about 60%.
tele-044.explication: Pooling the two trials, DOACs reduced ischaemic stroke by about 32% (relative risk around 0.68) and increased major bleeding by about 60%, with no difference in cardiovascular or all-cause mortality. The absolute benefit therefore depends on the patient's baseline thromboembolic and bleeding risks. This meta-analysis informed the class IIb recommendation in the 2024 ESC guidelines. The pitfall is to conclude "no effect" from NOAH-AFNET 6 alone, or "same effect as in clinical AF" from ARTESiA alone.
tele-044.aRetenir: Device-detected AF: DOACs = one third fewer ischaemic strokes, more bleeding, no effect on mortality.
tele-044.rappel: A meta-analysis pools trials to gain power and estimate an effect more precisely than a single trial, particularly when individual results appear to conflict. In device-detected AF, the effect of an anticoagulant is read on three outcomes: ischaemic stroke, major bleeding and mortality. The net benefit depends on the patient's baseline embolic risk and bleeding risk: it is more favourable the higher the embolic risk. This individualised reasoning, rather than a uniform rule, underlies a class IIb recommendation.

tele-045.question: An 80-year-old woman with hypertension and a pacemaker. Remote monitoring: a continuous 36-hour AF episode, typical EGM, patient asymptomatic, not anticoagulated, bleeding risk not high. What do you propose?
options: No immediate action: asymptomatic subclinical AF, review at the annual check
Long-term aspirin and reassessment after the next transmission
Refer to the emergency department for immediate electrical cardioversion before anticoagulation
Call the patient, obtain an ECG if possible and offer oral anticoagulation
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): an episode lasting more than 24 h is associated with a markedly increased stroke risk (ASSERT).
Incorrect: aspirin is not an alternative to anticoagulation.
Incorrect (over-reaction): asymptomatic patient, AF for more than 24 h: cardioversion without prior anticoagulation carries a risk of embolism.
Correct: episode >24 h, CHA2DS2-VA of 3: in practice it is treated as clinical AF.
tele-045.explication: In the ASSERT analysis by duration, only subclinical AF episodes lasting more than 24 hours were associated with a significant increase in stroke risk. The ARTESiA and NOAH-AFNET 6 trials in fact excluded episodes lasting more than 24 h. In this patient with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 3 (age ≥75 years = 2, hypertension = 1), most experts consider that such a long episode warrants anticoagulation, all the more so if it is confirmed on an ECG, which makes it clinical AF. Aspirin is not an alternative. Emergency cardioversion is not indicated in an asymptomatic patient, and AF lasting more than 24 h is not cardioverted without prior anticoagulation (or TOE).
tele-045.aRetenir: Device-detected AF >24 h in an at-risk patient: in practice it is treated as clinical AF.
tele-045.rappel: The duration of device-detected AF episodes modulates embolic risk: in ASSERT, only episodes lasting more than 24 hours were associated with a significant increase in stroke risk. Anticoagulation trials in subclinical AF excluded these prolonged episodes, so their conclusions do not apply to them. In practice, a long episode in an at-risk patient is managed as clinical AF, all the more so as it is often captured on an ECG. Cardioversion of AF lasting more than 24 hours requires at least 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation beforehand or a TOE.

tele-046.question: A 58-year-old pacemaker patient with no risk factors (CHA2DS2-VA = 0). Remote monitoring shows a single 40-second AF episode confirmed on the EGM. What is the appropriate management?
options: Immediate oral anticoagulation, since the episode is confirmed on the device EGM
Planned admission for cardioversion and aetiological work-up of AF
No anticoagulation; monitor AF burden, manage risk factors
Long-term aspirin, then review AF burden in one year
commentaires: Incorrect (over-reaction): a brief episode in a patient with no risk factors does not warrant anticoagulation.
Incorrect: cardioversion makes no sense for an asymptomatic 40-second episode that has already ended.
Correct: very low thromboembolic risk; monitor for progression and manage risk factors.
Incorrect: aspirin has no role in stroke prevention in AF.
tele-046.explication: A brief, isolated episode in a patient with no risk factors carries a very low thromboembolic risk: no evidence supports anticoagulation, and aspirin has no role in this setting. The 2024 ESC guidelines emphasise monitoring for progression (longer episodes, clinical AF) and managing risk factors and comorbidities (hypertension, weight, alcohol, sleep apnoea). Remote monitoring is precisely what allows the AF burden to be followed over time. Cardioversion makes no sense for an asymptomatic 40-second episode.
tele-046.aRetenir: Brief episode, CHA2DS2-VA of 0: no anticoagulation, monitor for progression.
tele-046.rappel: AF is a progressive disease: short episodes can lengthen, the burden can increase and AF can become clinical, persistent and then permanent. Remote monitoring makes it possible to follow this progression (episode duration, AF burden), which prompts reassessment of the anticoagulation decision. The ESC 2024 guidelines put the management of risk factors and comorbidities at the heart of AF treatment: hypertension, obesity, diabetes, alcohol consumption, sleep apnoea, physical inactivity. In a patient without risk factors, the embolic risk of a short episode is very low and does not justify anticoagulation.

tele-047.question: Dual-chamber pacemaker: numerous "AF episodes" with mode switching. On the EGM, the atrial channel senses, on every cycle, an event at a short, constant interval after each QRS, in addition to the sinus P wave. The ventricular rhythm is regular. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia triggered by a PVC
Far-field R-wave oversensing by the atrial lead
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction, every other F wave hidden
True paroxysmal AF, with anticoagulation to be discussed
commentaires: Incorrect: PMT causes ventricular pacing at the upper rate, not an atrial signal at a fixed coupling interval with a regular rhythm.
Correct: an atrial event at a fixed interval after each QRS is the hallmark of far-field R-wave sensing, which doubles the apparent atrial rate.
Incorrect: flutter would produce regular F waves independent of the QRS.
Incorrect: these false episodes must certainly not lead to anticoagulation.
tele-047.explication: An atrial event sensed at a fixed interval after each QRS, with otherwise regular sinus activity, is the hallmark of far-field sensing of the ventricular signal by the atrial lead. The apparent atrial rate doubles, crosses the atrial tachycardia detection threshold and triggers inappropriate mode switching and false "AF" episodes. The fix is to lengthen the post-ventricular atrial blanking period or reduce atrial sensitivity, without losing detection of true AF. These false episodes must certainly not lead to anticoagulation. 2:1 flutter would produce regular F waves independent of the QRS.
tele-047.aRetenir: Atrial event at a fixed coupling interval after each QRS = far-field R wave, not AF.
tele-047.rappel: The atrial lead can sense far-field ventricular activity (far-field R wave), particularly when it lies near the tricuspid annulus or when atrial sensitivity is high. The signal occurs at a fixed interval after every QRS, paced or intrinsic, and results in two atrial events being counted per cycle: the apparent atrial rate doubles, triggering false atrial tachyarrhythmia episodes and inappropriate mode switching. Correction relies on the post-ventricular atrial blanking period, far-field rejection functions or a cautious reduction in atrial sensitivity, while preserving sensing of low-amplitude AF signals.

tele-048.question: AF alert in a patient with a dual-chamber ICD. Which elements should you analyse?
options: The ventricular rate during AF and how close it comes to the VT/VF zones
Anticoagulation status and CHA2DS2-VA score
Any inappropriate therapies delivered
Whether to disable ICD therapies during AF episodes
Whether to program the device to DDD without mode switching to track the AF
commentaires: Correct: rapid AF close to the detection zones exposes the patient to inappropriate therapy.
Correct: thromboembolic risk is one of the three consequences to assess.
Correct: remote monitoring allows them to be identified, or even anticipated (ECOST).
Incorrect: disabling therapies would leave the patient unprotected; act on the rate and the programming instead.
Incorrect: without mode switching, the ventricle would be paced at the maximum tracking rate.
tele-048.explication: In an ICD patient, AF has three consequences to assess: thromboembolic risk (duration, burden, CHA2DS2-VA, anticoagulation), the risk of inappropriate therapy if the ventricular rate approaches the detection zones, and haemodynamic impact (HF, loss of BiV pacing with CRT). Remote monitoring makes it possible to act before an inappropriate shock, as ECOST showed, by controlling the rate and adjusting the programming (zones, discriminators); disabling therapies would leave the patient unprotected. Turning off mode switching to track AF in DDD would also be a mistake: the ventricle would be paced at the maximum tracking rate.
tele-048.aRetenir: AF in an ICD patient: thromboembolic risk, risk of inappropriate shock and impact on HF.
tele-048.rappel: In an ICD recipient, AF raises a specific problem: if the conducted ventricular rate reaches a VT or VF detection zone, the device may deliver inappropriate therapy. SVT–VT discriminators (RR stability, EGM morphology, comparison of atrial and ventricular rates in a dual-chamber device) apply mainly in the VT zone and are not infallible; in the VF zone, rate alone is usually enough to trigger therapy. Prevention relies on ventricular rate control in AF and appropriate programming (high-rate zones, prolonged detection durations), never on disabling therapies.

tele-049.question: A patient already anticoagulated for known paroxysmal AF. Remote monitoring has shown persistent AF (100% burden) for 3 weeks, with a mean ventricular rate of 75 bpm. The patient is asymptomatic. What level of urgency and what management?
options: No action: the patient is anticoagulated and rate-controlled, close the alert
Stop the anticoagulant by telephone, as the AF is now permanent and stable
Urgent: send the patient to the emergency department today for electrical cardioversion
Non-urgent: inform the responsible physician and book a visit (rhythm control)
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): doing nothing misses a window to restore sinus rhythm; this is a marker of progression.
Incorrect: thromboembolic risk does not fall when AF becomes persistent or permanent; stopping would be a serious error.
Incorrect (over-reaction): well-tolerated, rate-controlled AF in an anticoagulated patient: no life-threatening emergency.
Correct: non-critical alert; planned reassessment of rhythm control, checking adherence to anticoagulation.
tele-049.explication: Well-tolerated persistent AF with a controlled rate in a patient already anticoagulated is not life-threatening: the alert is reviewed within the usual time frame, is not critical, and warrants planned reassessment rather than immediate action. The 2024 ESC guidelines suggest considering rhythm control, especially if the AF is recent, and cardioversion requires at least 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or a TOE. Progression to persistent AF is also a marker of disease progression to be documented. Doing nothing would miss a window to restore sinus rhythm, and stopping the anticoagulant would be a serious error: thromboembolic risk does not fall when AF becomes permanent.
tele-049.aRetenir: Well-tolerated persistent AF on anticoagulation: non-urgent, but planned reassessment of rhythm control.
tele-049.rappel: AF is classified by duration: paroxysmal (terminating spontaneously or with intervention within 7 days), persistent (beyond 7 days), long-standing persistent (more than 12 months, with a rhythm-control strategy still considered) and permanent (a shared decision not to attempt further restoration of sinus rhythm). Moving from one form to the next reflects disease progression. Anticoagulation depends on thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VA), not on the type of AF. Cardioversion of AF lasting more than 24 hours requires at least 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or a TOE.

tele-050.question: In an ARTESiA subgroup analysis (Lancet Neurol 2025), how did patients with prior stroke or TIA fare?
options: A higher stroke risk on aspirin, hence a greater absolute benefit
Apixaban paradoxically increased the risk of haemorrhagic stroke
The same relative and absolute benefit as the other patients
They were excluded from the trial because their stroke risk was deemed too high
commentaires: Correct: higher stroke risk on aspirin, greater absolute benefit of apixaban (subgroup analysis).
Incorrect: apixaban reduced strokes in this subgroup.
Incorrect: as their baseline risk was higher, the absolute benefit was greater.
Incorrect: they were included, as a minority, and were the subject of a subgroup analysis.
tele-050.explication: Patients with prior stroke or TIA made up a minority of ARTESiA participants but had a higher stroke risk on aspirin. Apixaban reduced strokes in this subgroup, with a greater absolute benefit than in the other patients. This illustrates the general principle of the 2024 ESC guidelines: in subclinical AF, the decision to anticoagulate depends on individual thromboembolic risk, which is highest in patients with a history of cerebrovascular events. These results nonetheless come from a subgroup analysis.
tele-050.aRetenir: Subclinical AF with prior stroke/TIA: higher risk, greater absolute benefit from DOACs.
tele-050.rappel: The absolute benefit of a preventive treatment depends on the patient's baseline risk: for the same relative reduction, the higher the initial risk, the greater the number of events prevented. In AF, prior stroke or TIA is one of the strongest embolic risk factors, which is why it carries 2 points in the CHA2DS2-VA score. A subgroup analysis nevertheless remains exploratory: it generates hypotheses and nuances the interpretation of a trial, without the evidential weight of the primary endpoint.

tele-051.question: Dual-chamber pacemaker; the measured P-wave amplitude on the atrial lead has fallen from 2.5 to 0.6 mV. The AF burden counter reads 3%, whereas the clinic ECG shows AF. What is the explanation and what is the risk?
options: Far-field R-wave oversensing: AF burden overestimated by the counter
Battery depletion: the AF counter shuts down to save energy
AF undersensing: burden underestimated, falsely reassuring decision
Reliable counter: the AF was brief and the ECG happened to catch the episode
commentaires: Incorrect: far-field oversensing instead leads to overestimation of the burden.
Incorrect: nothing suggests battery depletion.
Correct: with a 0.6 mV P wave, the small AF potentials fall below the sensing threshold or into the blanking period.
Incorrect: a counter is only reliable if atrial sensing is good, which is no longer the case here.
tele-051.explication: AF electrograms are of low and highly variable amplitude. When atrial sensing is degraded, some signals fall below the sensitivity threshold and others fall into the post-ventricular blanking periods: the device no longer counts all the AF, the burden is underestimated and mode switching may be intermittent, with periods of irregular tracking. In remote monitoring, a low burden is therefore only reliable if atrial sensing is good. Atrial sensitivity should be checked and, if necessary, cautiously increased (watching for far-field sensing), and the anticoagulation decision should rely on the ECG. Far-field oversensing instead leads to overestimation.
tele-051.aRetenir: Poor atrial sensing leads to underestimation of AF burden: do not be reassured by the counter.
tele-051.rappel: The quality of atrial sensing determines the reliability of all the device's atrial diagnostics: AF burden, stored episodes and mode switching. AF electrograms are of low and highly variable amplitude; a fall in the measured P-wave amplitude (displacement, fibrosis, progression of atrial disease) leads to undersensing. Some signals also fall within post-ventricular blanking periods, particularly at high ventricular rates. Increasing atrial sensitivity improves sensing but at the risk of far-field R-wave oversensing, so both must be checked.

tele-052.question: In a patient with a cardiac implantable electronic device and subclinical AF confirmed on the EGM (with no AF on ECG), which factors favour oral anticoagulation?
options: Prior stroke or TIA
Episodes lasting more than 24 hours
High CHA2DS2-VA score
High bleeding risk
Single 20-second episode
commentaires: Correct: the absolute benefit of apixaban was greater in this ARTESiA subgroup.
Correct: episodes >24 h were associated with an increased stroke risk in ASSERT.
Correct: the benefit increases with thromboembolic risk.
Incorrect: a high bleeding risk weighs against; the 2024 ESC guidelines exclude these patients from the class IIb recommendation.
Incorrect: a single episode lasting a few seconds has no demonstrated thromboembolic significance.
tele-052.explication: The benefit of anticoagulation in subclinical AF is modest on average (NOAH-AFNET 6/ARTESiA meta-analysis: about one third fewer ischaemic strokes, more major bleeding); it grows as thromboembolic risk rises. Prior stroke/TIA (greater absolute benefit in the ARTESiA subgroup), a high CHA2DS2-VA score and long episodes (>24 h, associated with increased risk in ASSERT) point towards anticoagulation. A high bleeding risk, by contrast, weighs against it: the 2024 ESC guidelines explicitly exclude these patients from the class IIb recommendation. A single episode lasting a few seconds has no demonstrated thromboembolic significance.
tele-052.aRetenir: Subclinical AF: anticoagulation is weighed according to thromboembolic risk (prior stroke, CHA2DS2-VA, duration) and bleeding risk.
tele-052.rappel: The decision to anticoagulate in subclinical AF rests on an individual balance. On the benefit side: a high embolic risk (high CHA2DS2-VA score, prior stroke or TIA) and a high arrhythmia burden, particularly episodes lasting more than 24 hours, which come close to clinical AF. On the risk side: high bleeding risk, assessed by looking for modifiable factors (uncontrolled hypertension, concomitant antiplatelet or NSAID, alcohol). Very short, isolated episodes have no proven embolic significance and call for monitoring.

tele-053.question: An ICD patient calls the clinic: he received a single shock an hour ago and feels well, with no pain or presyncope. What do you advise?
options: Call the emergency services (15 in France) immediately for medical transport and an urgent device check
Nothing to do: the ICD did its job, mention it at the next scheduled check
Send a manual transmission for prompt review; call back if another shock or symptoms occur
Place the magnet on the device to prevent another shock, then wait for the clinic to call
commentaires: Incorrect (over-reaction): a single well-tolerated shock is not a life-threatening emergency.
Incorrect (under-reaction): every shock must be analysed; even if appropriate, it may reveal ischaemia, hypokalaemia or decompensation.
Correct: a single well-tolerated shock warrants prompt EGM review (2023 HRS consensus); call the emergency services (15) for multiple shocks or symptoms.
Incorrect: the magnet suspends all protection and should only be used under medical supervision, once the diagnosis is established.
tele-053.explication: A single, well-tolerated shock in a patient who feels well is not a life-threatening emergency but must be analysed promptly, as recommended by the 2023 HRS consensus. The key question is whether it was an appropriate shock for VT/VF, or an inappropriate one for rapid AF, sinus tachycardia, oversensing or lead noise. The transmission, manual or automatic (depending on the system, the transmission after a shock is initiated by the patient or sent automatically), provides the episode EGM. By contrast, multiple shocks, a shock followed by symptoms (pain, breathlessness, syncope) or an electrical storm call for the emergency services (15). Ignoring the shock would be a mistake: even if appropriate, it may reveal ischaemia, hypokalaemia or decompensation. Applying a magnet at home would leave the patient without any protection and without a diagnosis.
tele-053.aRetenir: Single well-tolerated shock: transmission and prompt review; multiple shocks or symptoms: emergency services (15).
tele-053.rappel: Every ICD shock must be analysed on the episode EGM to distinguish an appropriate shock (VT or VF) from an inappropriate one (fast SVT, oversensing, lead noise). Management depends on the number of shocks and on tolerance: a single shock in a patient who feels well warrants a transmission and prompt analysis, whereas multiple shocks or a shock followed by symptoms (chest pain, breathlessness, syncope) require the emergency services. Even when appropriate, a shock calls for a search for a trigger (ischaemia, potassium disorder, decompensation, adherence). A magnet, which suspends therapies in most ICDs, is used only under medical supervision.

tele-054.question: An ICD patient reports three shocks in one hour and feels unwell. What should be done?
options: Place a magnet on the device to suspend shocks and wait for improvement
Call the emergency services (15 in France): multiple shocks with symptoms are urgent
Send a manual transmission and wait for the remote monitoring clinic to call back
Contact the usual cardiologist for an early clinic appointment within the week
commentaires: Incorrect: the magnet should only be used under medical supervision; in an electrical storm, it removes life-saving protection.
Correct: electrical storm or repeated inappropriate shocks, both emergencies; the symptomatic patient calls the emergency services (15).
Incorrect (under-reaction): remote monitoring is not an emergency service; review may wait until the working day.
Incorrect (under-reaction): multiple shocks with feeling unwell = immediate emergency, not a deferred appointment.
tele-054.explication: Multiple shocks in quick succession, especially with symptoms, require emergency care by the SAMU (French emergency medical service): this may be an electrical storm, which is life-threatening, or repeated inappropriate shocks (lead noise, rapid AF) that must be stopped. In hospital, device interrogation guides treatment: sedation, correction of triggers, antiarrhythmic drugs, temporary deactivation of therapies if they are inappropriate. A magnet suspends therapies in most ICDs, but should only be used under medical supervision and once the diagnosis is established. The 2023 HRS consensus classifies multiple shocks as critical ("red") alerts, but remote monitoring is not an emergency service: the symptomatic patient calls the emergency services (15).
tele-054.aRetenir: Multiple shocks = call the emergency services (15), without waiting for remote monitoring.
tele-054.rappel: Placing a magnet over an ICD suspends tachyarrhythmia detection, and therefore therapies, in most models, without changing bradycardia pacing; the effect ends when the magnet is removed. It is used to stop inappropriate shocks (lead noise, oversensing, fast SVT) or to protect a procedure exposed to interference, always with ECG monitoring and an external defibrillator available. In electrical storm, it would deprive the patient of life-saving protection. Determining the type of shocks relies on interrogation of the device in a medical setting.

tele-055.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, how is electrical storm defined in an ICD patient?
options: At least 3 shocks, appropriate or not, over a one-month period
More than 100 PVCs per hour on a 24-hour Holter
At least 3 episodes of non-sustained VT of more than 10 beats in 24 h
At least 3 episodes of sustained VT/VF treated within 24 hours
commentaires: Incorrect: the definition refers to 24 hours and to true arrhythmias, not to inappropriate shocks.
Incorrect: frequent PVCs do not define electrical storm.
Incorrect: non-sustained VT does not meet the definition.
Correct: at least 3 separate episodes of sustained VT/VF within 24 h requiring therapy (ATP or shock).
tele-055.explication: Electrical storm is defined as at least 3 separate episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within 24 hours; in an ICD patient, these are episodes requiring therapy (ATP or shock). It is an emergency associated with excess mortality, requiring hospital admission, a search for a trigger (ischaemia, potassium disturbance, HF, drugs) and often beta-blockers, amiodarone, sedation or even ablation. Frequent PVCs, non-sustained VT, shocks spread over several weeks or inappropriate shocks do not meet this definition. Remote monitoring may reveal ATP-treated episodes that the patient did not feel.
tele-055.aRetenir: Electrical storm = ≥3 treated sustained VT/VF episodes in 24 h: hospital admission.
tele-055.rappel: Electrical storm is defined as at least 3 distinct episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within 24 hours, separated by at least 5 minutes, requiring intervention (in an ICD recipient: ATP or shock). It is managed in hospital: identification and correction of triggers (ischaemia, potassium disorder, heart failure decompensation, proarrhythmic drugs), beta-blocker and amiodarone, sedation to reduce adrenergic drive, ICD reprogramming if needed, and catheter ablation in case of failure or recurrent monomorphic VT. Incessant VT, which persists despite therapies, is a particular form.

tele-056.question: ICD remote monitoring: a single episode of monomorphic VT at 190 bpm, terminated by one ATP burst; the patient is asymptomatic and felt nothing. No other episodes. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Close the alert without calling: ATP worked and the patient felt nothing
Call the patient, look for a trigger and inform the responsible physician
Disable ATP at the next visit to avoid VT acceleration
Send the patient to the emergency department for admission, as for electrical storm
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): VT is an event that may reveal ischaemia, a potassium disturbance, decompensation or non-adherence.
Correct: effective appropriate therapy, a prompt but non-life-threatening alert; look for a cause and review treatment.
Incorrect: ATP was effective and prevents shocks; disabling it would be harmful.
Incorrect (over-reaction): a single episode is not an electrical storm (≥3 in 24 h).
tele-056.explication: A single VT terminated by ATP shows that the ICD is working and is not an electrical storm. It should not, however, be closed without action: it is an arrhythmic event that may reveal ischaemia, a potassium disturbance, decompensation or non-adherence. Calling the patient and reviewing treatment (beta-blocker, antiarrhythmic drug, considering ablation if episodes recur) are indicated. ATP reduces the number of shocks and disabling it would be harmful. The level of urgency increases with recurrence, symptoms or shocks.
tele-056.aRetenir: VT treated by ATP: neither panic nor closing the alert; look for the cause and seek the responsible physician's opinion.
tele-056.rappel: Antitachycardia pacing (ATP) delivers a burst or ramp of pulses slightly faster than the VT, which penetrate the re-entry circuit and terminate it painlessly. It terminates most fast monomorphic VTs and reduces the number of shocks; the risk of VT acceleration exists but is low. Every treated episode, even if not felt, is a ventricular arrhythmia that warrants a search for a trigger and a review of treatment. Recurrence prompts optimisation of antiarrhythmic therapy and consideration of ablation, whereas electrical storm requires hospital admission.

tele-057.question: Single-chamber ICD: a shock was delivered for an irregular tachycardia at 210 bpm, with EGM morphology identical to that of the baseline rhythm and highly variable RR intervals. The patient has known paroxysmal AF. What do you conclude and what do you do?
options: Appropriate shock for polymorphic VT: hospital admission and intravenous amiodarone
Inappropriate shock for rapid AF: slow the rate, check anticoagulation, reprogram
Lead noise: urgent admission and surgical revision of the RV lead
T-wave oversensing: reduce the ICD's ventricular sensitivity
commentaires: Incorrect: polymorphic VT would change the EGM morphology, which here is identical to the baseline rhythm.
Correct: an irregular tachycardia with the same morphology as the conducted rhythm in a patient with AF = inappropriate shock for rapid AF.
Incorrect: noise would produce very short, non-physiological intervals and a non-cardiac signal.
Incorrect: T-wave oversensing produces alternating signals at a fixed interval, not highly variable RR intervals.
tele-057.explication: An irregular tachycardia whose morphology is identical to that of the conducted rhythm, in a patient with paroxysmal AF, points to rapidly conducted AF: the shock is inappropriate. Management combines rate or rhythm control, anticoagulation according to CHA2DS2-VA and optimised programming (higher detection zone, longer detection durations, morphology and stability discriminators), as in MADIT-RIT. Remote monitoring allows rapid AF to be spotted before the shock, hence the reduction in inappropriate shocks in ECOST. Lead noise would produce very short, non-physiological intervals and a non-cardiac signal.
tele-057.aRetenir: Irregular tachycardia with the same morphology as the baseline rhythm = rapid AF: inappropriate shock.
tele-057.rappel: SVT–VT discrimination in an ICD relies on a few criteria. Stability: AF produces irregular RR intervals, monomorphic VT regular cycles. Morphology: a ventricular EGM identical to the template of conducted rhythm points to a supraventricular origin. Onset: sudden for VT, gradual for sinus tachycardia. In a dual-chamber device, comparison of atrial and ventricular rates is added. In a single-chamber device, only ventricular criteria are available. These discriminators apply mainly in the VT zone, hence the importance of sufficiently high detection zones and prolonged detection durations.

tele-058.question: A secondary prevention ICD patient on amiodarone. For the past week, remote monitoring has shown repeated episodes of monomorphic VT at 140 bpm, lasting several minutes, in a monitor-only zone below the lowest therapy zone (150 bpm): no therapy delivered. The patient reports exertional breathlessness. What do you do?
options: See the patient promptly: symptomatic slow VT, therapy zone and ablation
Stop the amiodarone, which slows the VT below the zone, and review in 3 months
Program a shock zone at 130 bpm straight away without ATP, then review in 6 months
No action: these VTs were not treated by the ICD, so they are well tolerated
commentaires: Correct: repeated symptomatic slow VT; document it, consider a therapy zone with ATP, drug treatment and ablation.
Incorrect: stopping the antiarrhythmic drug would lead to faster and more frequent VT.
Incorrect: a 130 bpm shock zone without ATP would shock exercise-induced sinus tachycardia and VTs that ATP would have terminated.
Incorrect (under-reaction): the absence of therapy does not mean the absence of severity; the patient is symptomatic.
tele-058.explication: Amiodarone slows VT, which may fall below the lowest therapy zone and merely be recorded in a monitor zone, without therapy. Prolonged, repeated, symptomatic slow VT can cause haemodynamic deterioration and heart failure decompensation. The patient should be seen promptly, the VT documented, and an additional therapy zone with ATP considered (taking care not to treat exercise-induced sinus tachycardia), as well as ablation, which is the option of choice for recurrent VT in ischaemic cardiomyopathy despite amiodarone. The absence of therapy does not mean the absence of severity.
tele-058.aRetenir: Slow VT below the therapy zone: no therapy does not mean no problem.
tele-058.rappel: An ICD treats a tachycardia only if its rate reaches a therapy zone; below that, a monitor zone can only store the episodes. Antiarrhythmic drugs, amiodarone in particular, slow VT and can bring it below the lowest zone, so that it persists untreated. Prolonged slow VT may be poorly tolerated and lead to heart failure decompensation. Creating a slow VT zone with ATP must take into account the overlap with exercise-induced sinus tachycardia or AF, and must therefore be combined with discriminators. Ablation is the treatment of choice for recurrent monomorphic VT in ischaemic heart disease despite amiodarone.

tele-059.question: True or false: in MADIT-RIT, ICD programming with a high-rate therapy zone (≥200 bpm) reduced inappropriate therapies and all-cause mortality compared with conventional programming.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: high-rate programming = inappropriate therapies reduced by about 80% and all-cause mortality reduced (HR 0.45).
Incorrect: MADIT-RIT did show both benefits for high-rate programming.
tele-059.explication: MADIT-RIT randomised 1500 primary prevention patients to three programming strategies: conventional (therapy from 170 bpm after 2.5 s), high-rate (therapy only from 200 bpm) or delayed detection (delays of 60 s, 12 s or 2.5 s depending on rate). Both strategies markedly reduced first inappropriate therapies (by about 80%). High-rate programming also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0.45); with delayed detection, the mortality reduction was of similar magnitude but not significant (HR 0.56, p = 0.06). This result underpins current programming recommendations, which give non-sustained VT time to terminate spontaneously. In remote monitoring, this means that many brief episodes are recorded without being treated: this is intentional.
tele-059.aRetenir: MADIT-RIT: higher detection rate or longer detection = far fewer inappropriate therapies; mortality reduced with the high-rate strategy.
tele-059.rappel: Modern ICD programming aims to limit unnecessary therapies: many fast episodes are non-sustained VTs that stop spontaneously, or SVTs. The two levers are a high detection rate (therapy reserved for the fastest rates) and a prolonged detection duration (therapy only if the arrhythmia persists), supplemented by SVT–VT discriminators and ATP before charging. Avoiding unnecessary therapies spares the patient painful shocks and saves battery, with no demonstrated loss of protection. On remote monitoring, it is therefore normal to see stored episodes without therapy.

tele-060.question: ICD: an episode classified as "VF" triggered a shock. The near-field ventricular EGM shows, in sinus rhythm at 95 bpm, two sensed signals per cycle, alternating between a large-amplitude signal (QRS) and a small rounded signal occurring about 300 ms later. What is the diagnosis?
options: T-wave oversensing (double counting), inappropriate shock
Far-field P-wave oversensing by the RV defibrillation lead
True VF, appropriately treated by the first delivered shock
Electromagnetic interference from a nearby mobile phone
commentaires: Correct: two signals per cycle, QRS then a rounded wave at a fixed interval: 95 → 190 bpm counted.
Incorrect: the second signal occurs about 300 ms after the QRS, at the time of repolarisation, not of the P wave.
Incorrect: the underlying rhythm is sinus at 95 bpm; the counted rate is artificially doubled.
Incorrect: interference would produce a non-physiological high-frequency signal.
tele-060.explication: Two signals per cycle, alternating between the QRS and a slow rounded repolarisation wave at a fixed interval, indicate T-wave oversensing. The counted rate doubles (95 → 190 bpm), which may reach the VF zone and trigger an inappropriate shock. Predisposing factors are a small R wave (automatically increased sensitivity), large T waves (hyperkalaemia, long QT, Brugada) or changes in repolarisation. Correction involves changing the sensitivity or filtering, a T-wave rejection algorithm, a change of sensing vector or lead revision. Interference would produce a non-physiological high-frequency signal.
tele-060.aRetenir: Two alternating signals per cycle at a fixed interval = T-wave oversensing.
tele-060.rappel: An ICD adjusts its ventricular sensitivity automatically: after each sensed event, the sensing threshold starts at a fraction of the R-wave amplitude and then decays towards the maximum programmed sensitivity, so as to detect low-amplitude VF signals. This behaviour exposes the device to T-wave oversensing, particularly when the R wave is small or the T wave large (hyperkalaemia, long QT, Brugada, repolarisation changes). Regular double counting (R then T at a fixed interval) doubles the measured rate. Corrective options involve sensitivity, filtering, T-wave rejection algorithms, the sensing vector or the lead.

tele-061.question: Propose three urgency levels for triaging ICD remote monitoring alerts and give two examples of each.
tele-061.reponseAttendue: Level 1, critical ("red" alert in the 2023 HRS consensus, handled as a priority the same day, immediate contact, possibly the emergency services, 15 in France): multiple shocks, noise on the ICD lead, out-of-range shock or RV pacing impedance, VF detection or therapies disabled, battery end of life or device reset. Level 2, important ("yellow" alert, reviewed within the working day with prompt action): single shock, VT treated by ATP, AF burden or ventricular rate during AF above thresholds, fall in % BiV pacing, out-of-range pacing threshold, ERI (plan replacement), HF alert. Level 3, non-actionable (information already known, to be reviewed at the scheduled check, with alerts reprogrammed to reduce their number): known persistent AF, already anticoagulated and controlled; brief AF episodes already known in a low-risk patient. Context changes the level: in a pacemaker-dependent patient, loss of capture, abnormal RV impedance or noise become critical.
tele-061.explication: The 2023 HRS consensus distinguishes "red" alerts, critical because they may deprive the patient of therapy (ICD lead malfunction, depleted battery, therapies disabled, multiple shocks), from "yellow" alerts, important because early review may change management (single shock, ATP, AF, % pacing, thresholds, ERI). It asks for all alerts to be handled within the working day, prioritising red ones, and for non-actionable alerts to be reprogrammed to avoid overload. Each clinic translates these principles into its own protocol, according to its resources and review hours. Patient context matters: a threshold rise does not carry the same urgency in a pacemaker-dependent patient as in one who is not. The examples given here are indicative.
tele-061.aRetenir: Effective triage assigns each alert a level (critical, important, non-actionable) and a response time, adapted to the patient's context.
tele-061.rappel: Triage of device alerts is based on the potential clinical consequence of each event. Critical alerts are those that may deprive the patient of therapy or reveal a life-threatening problem: ICD lead dysfunction, a shock circuit fault, a depleted battery, disabled therapies, multiple shocks. Important alerts are those for which early review may change management: a single shock, ATP, AF, loss of BiV pacing, thresholds, ERI, HF alerts. Non-actionable alerts should be reprogrammed to avoid overload. The patient's context, particularly pacemaker dependence, can raise an alert by one level.

tele-062.question: Dual-chamber ICD: on the EGM of a tachycardia at 180 bpm, which features favour VT over supraventricular tachycardia?
options: Ventricular rate faster than the atrial rate
Ventricular EGM morphology different from that of the baseline rhythm
Atrioventricular dissociation
Atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate with irregular RR intervals
Gradual onset, in parallel with sinus acceleration
commentaires: Correct: V > A indicates VT in the vast majority of cases.
Correct: a change in morphology relative to the baseline template is a strong argument.
Correct: AV dissociation is a strong argument for VT.
Incorrect: A > V with irregular RR intervals suggests conducted AF or atrial flutter.
Incorrect: a gradual onset in parallel with sinus acceleration suggests sinus tachycardia.
tele-062.explication: An atrial channel allows atrial and ventricular rates to be compared: V > A indicates VT in the vast majority of cases. A change in ventricular EGM morphology relative to the baseline rhythm template and AV dissociation are also strong arguments. Conversely, an atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate with irregular RR intervals suggests conducted AF or atrial flutter, and a gradual onset in parallel with sinus acceleration suggests sinus tachycardia. The pitfall is VT with 1:1 retrograde conduction (A = V), where morphology and mode of onset become decisive.
tele-062.aRetenir: V > A, different morphology and AV dissociation = VT; irregular A > V or gradual onset = supraventricular origin.
tele-062.rappel: In a dual-chamber ICD, analysis of a tachycardia starts with the relationship between atrial and ventricular rates. V > A indicates VT in the vast majority of cases; A > V points to SVT (conducted AF, atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia), without excluding coexisting VT; A = V (1:1) is the most difficult situation, which relies on ventricular EGM morphology, the mode of onset (initiating atrial or ventricular event, sudden or gradual) and stability. AV dissociation and a change in morphology from the baseline rhythm template are strong arguments for VT.

tele-063.question: Impedance alert: the RV lead pacing impedance has risen abruptly from 550 Ω to over 2500 Ω. What is the main hypothesis?
options: Hyperkalaemia with raised thresholds
Lead insulation breach
Conductor fracture or connection problem
Normal lead maturation
commentaires: Incorrect: hyperkalaemia alters the capture threshold, not lead impedance.
Incorrect: an insulation breach instead lowers impedance (current leak).
Correct: soaring impedance reflects a conductor fracture or poor contact at the connector.
Incorrect: maturation alters the threshold in the first weeks, not impedance to this extent.
tele-063.explication: An abrupt rise in impedance beyond the usual limits (typically above 1500–2000 Ω depending on the lead) points to a conductor fracture or poor contact at the connector (loose set screw). An insulation breach, by contrast, lowers impedance through current leakage. Maturation of the electrode–tissue interface alters the threshold in the first weeks, but not impedance to this extent. The risk is loss of capture and, in an ICD, noise sensing with inappropriate shocks.
tele-063.aRetenir: Soaring impedance = conductor fracture or faulty connection.
tele-063.rappel: Lead pacing impedance usually lies between about 200 and 2,000 Ω depending on the model, and its trend matters more than a single value. A sudden rise, or a value beyond the limits, points to conductor fracture or a connection fault at the header; a fall points to an insulation breach. An abnormal impedance is often accompanied by threshold changes, loss of capture or noise on the sensing channel. In an ICD, such noise exposes the patient to inappropriate shocks, which makes an impedance alert on a defibrillation lead particularly urgent.

tele-064.question: Pacemaker: the bipolar atrial lead impedance has gradually fallen from 480 Ω to 190 Ω. What is the main hypothesis?
options: Conductor fracture
Lead dislodgement
Battery end of life
Insulation breach
commentaires: Incorrect: a fracture raises impedance.
Incorrect: dislodgement mainly affects threshold and sensing.
Incorrect: the battery does not alter lead impedance; it is the other way round, as the insulation breach drains it faster.
Correct: collapsing impedance (below 200–250 Ω) reflects current leakage through damaged insulation.
tele-064.explication: A fall in impedance, particularly below 200–250 Ω, reflects current leakage through damaged insulation (wear from friction, subclavian crush, abrasion in the pocket). It increases current drain and therefore battery depletion, and can cause loss of capture or oversensing. Lead dislodgement mainly affects threshold and sensing, and a fracture raises impedance. Trends should be compared, pacing and sensing checked, and reprogramming (a unipolar configuration as a temporary fix, depending on the defect) or lead revision considered.
tele-064.rappel: Lead insulation separates the conductors from each other and from the surrounding tissue. An insulation breach (abrasion in the pocket, friction against the can or another lead, crush between the clavicle and the first rib) creates a current leak that lowers the measured impedance, often gradually. The consequences are increased battery drain, loss of capture through current shunting and oversensing of spurious potentials. A fall in impedance is always read on the trend, with checks of threshold and sensing; depending on the conductor involved, unipolar reconfiguration may serve as a temporary fix until revision.

tele-065.question: ICD: noise alert on the RV lead. The near-field EGM shows irregular high-frequency signals with intervals of 120–150 ms, not visible on the shock (far-field) EGM. Numerous very brief "non-sustained VT" episodes. No shocks yet. What should be done?
options: Non-urgent: check the lead at the next annual visit, as no shock has been delivered
Reassure: these are non-sustained VTs; increase the beta-blocker and review in one month
Switch to weekly transmissions to follow the noise before taking action
Contact the patient the same day and have them seen without delay for a check and revision
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): an inappropriate shock can occur at any moment; the absence of shocks is not reassuring.
Incorrect: these are not true VTs but noise (120–150 ms intervals, near-field only).
Incorrect (under-reaction): monitoring without acting leaves the patient exposed to shocks and a failing lead.
Correct: a "red" alert; see the patient the same day, adjust therapies under ECG monitoring, then revise the lead.
tele-065.explication: Non-physiological intervals (below about 150 ms), a high-frequency signal visible on the near-field EGM but absent from the far-field EGM, and very short non-sustained VTs are the classic signs of a defibrillation lead fracture. The risk is an inappropriate shock at any moment, or even repeated shocks, as well as loss of protection if the lead fails. The 2023 HRS consensus classifies noise on an ICD lead as a critical ("red") alert: the patient must be seen the same day; therapies can be temporarily adjusted under continuous ECG monitoring, and lead revision is usually required. These signals are not true non-sustained VTs. Swerdlow showed that an early detection algorithm reduced fracture-related inappropriate shocks.
tele-065.aRetenir: ICD lead noise (intervals <150 ms, near-field only) = same-day emergency.
tele-065.rappel: An ICD records two types of ventricular EGM: the near-field EGM (bipolar, between tip and ring or distal coil), used for sensing, and the far-field EGM, recorded between the shock electrodes and reflecting global ventricular activity. Fracture or connection noise usually affects the sensing channel only: the shock EGM then shows the normal baseline rhythm. Non-physiological intervals, an intermittent, saturating signal and very short non-sustained VTs are the markers of noise. In an ICD recipient, it exposes the patient to inappropriate shocks at any time.

tele-066.question: What does Medtronic's Lead Integrity Alert (LIA) algorithm do when it is triggered?
options: Alert (audible and remote) and extension of VF detection
Permanent deactivation of all therapies until the device check
Automatic switch to another defibrillation configuration
Automatic increase of RV pacing amplitude to its maximum value
commentaires: Correct: it alerts the patient and the clinic and extends the number of intervals to detect VF; the situation remains urgent.
Incorrect: it does not disable therapies, which would leave the patient unprotected.
Incorrect: it neither replaces nor bypasses the failing lead.
Incorrect: LIA does not change the pacing amplitude.
tele-066.explication: LIA combines several indicators of lead fracture: abnormal impedance or an abrupt change, non-sustained VT episodes with very short intervals, and a short-interval counter (sensing integrity counter). When triggered, it alerts the patient and the clinic and automatically extends the number of intervals needed to detect VF, buying time to intervene before an inappropriate shock. Swerdlow showed that this algorithm reduced inappropriate shocks due to lead fracture. It does not disable therapies and does not replace lead revision: an LIA alert remains an emergency.
tele-066.aRetenir: Medtronic LIA: alert + extended VF detection, but the situation remains urgent.
tele-066.rappel: Algorithms monitoring the integrity of defibrillation leads combine several indicators of fracture: abnormal impedance or a sudden change, a counter of very short, non-physiological ventricular intervals, and non-sustained VT episodes with very short cycles. Their aim is to detect the dysfunction before the first inappropriate shock. When triggered, they alert the patient and the clinic and may automatically modify detection to delay therapy on noise, without disabling protection. They buy time but do not correct the fault: lead revision is still required.

tele-067.question: Pacemaker-dependent patient (complete AV block with no escape rhythm). Alert: RV pacing threshold has risen from 0.75 V to 3.0 V at 0.4 ms, with a programmed amplitude of 3.5 V. Implanted 3 weeks ago. What level of urgency?
options: Review at the 3-month check: the programmed amplitude is still above threshold
No action: a threshold rise at 3 weeks is a normal inflammatory reaction
Emergency ambulance admission for urgent insertion of a temporary pacing wire
Urgent: same-day contact, increase the amplitude and look for dislodgement
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): the margin is now only 0.5 V in a dependent patient; any further rise would cause asystole.
Incorrect (under-reaction): although inflammation is possible, the margin is insufficient and micro-dislodgement must be sought.
Incorrect (over-reaction): capture is still maintained; increasing the amplitude the same day is sufficient pending further assessment.
Correct: pacemaker dependence + near-zero margin = same-day action, then check the lead position.
tele-067.explication: An early threshold rise may reflect an inflammatory reaction at the interface or micro-dislodgement of the lead. Here the safety margin is now only 0.5 V, whereas the usual target is at least twice the threshold voltage. In a pacemaker-dependent patient, any further rise would cause loss of capture and asystole. Action is needed the same day: increase the amplitude, check the lead position and consider revision if the threshold keeps rising. As long as capture is maintained, emergency insertion of a temporary pacing wire is not necessary. The 2023 HRS consensus classifies threshold alerts as "yellow" alerts, but pacemaker dependence and a near-zero margin justify prioritising them here. The same figure would be less urgent in a patient with an escape rhythm.
tele-067.aRetenir: Threshold rise + pacemaker dependence = same-day emergency.
tele-067.rappel: The pacing safety margin is classically programmed to at least twice the threshold voltage (or three times the pulse width), to cover threshold fluctuations. After implantation, the threshold may rise transiently through an inflammatory reaction at the electrode–tissue interface, a phenomenon reduced by steroid-eluting electrodes; a large or sudden rise prompts a search for microdislodgement. The severity of loss of capture depends on the underlying rhythm: in a pacemaker-dependent patient, it causes asystole. Automatic capture management algorithms adjust the output when programmed in adaptive mode.

tele-068.question: True or false: in a patient who is not pacemaker-dependent, a moderate rise in atrial threshold, with a safety margin that is still adequate, requires urgent lead revision.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: adequate margin and a non-dependent patient: monitor the trend and adjust the amplitude if needed.
Correct: loss of atrial capture would at worst cause loss of AV synchrony, without asystole; not urgent.
tele-068.explication: If the safety margin remains adequate and the patient is not dependent, the situation is not urgent: the trend is monitored, the threshold checked at a transmission or scheduled visit, and the amplitude adjusted if needed. Loss of atrial capture would at worst cause loss of AV synchrony, without asystole. Lead dislodgement should nonetheless be sought if the rise is early or abrupt, and the impact on the battery monitored if the amplitude has to be increased. The level of urgency always depends on the clinical consequence of loss of capture.
tele-068.aRetenir: The urgency of a threshold alert depends on the patient's pacing dependence and the remaining margin.
tele-068.rappel: The consequence of loss of capture depends on the chamber and on the underlying rhythm. Loss of atrial capture deprives the patient of AV synchrony, with at most a fall in cardiac output or pacemaker syndrome. Loss of ventricular capture in a patient without a reliable escape rhythm causes asystole. Increasing the amplitude to preserve the margin has an energy cost that shortens battery longevity. The threshold trend and the time since implantation help to distinguish an interface reaction from displacement.

tele-069.question: Which of the following point to lead noise rather than a true ventricular arrhythmia on an ICD EGM?
options: Very short, non-physiological intervals (below about 150 ms)
Signals visible on the near-field EGM but absent from the far-field (shock) EGM
Regular intervals of around 300 ms, identical from one cycle to the next
Gradual onset with acceleration, then a stable morphology visible on all channels
Occurrence during arm movements or manipulation of the device
commentaires: Correct: such intervals are incompatible with myocardial activity.
Correct: the shock channel shows the normal baseline rhythm; this is the most useful argument.
Incorrect: regular cycles of around 300 ms suggest true monomorphic VT (200 bpm).
Incorrect: a plausible onset and consistent morphology on all channels suggest a true arrhythmia.
Correct: noise is often reproduced by manoeuvres (shoulder movement, pressure on the pocket).
tele-069.explication: Lead noise is recognised by intervals incompatible with myocardial activity and a sometimes saturating signal, confined to the near-field channel (the far-field shock EGM shows a normal baseline rhythm), often associated with a change in impedance and reproduced by manoeuvres (shoulder movement, pressure on the pocket). A true ventricular arrhythmia, by contrast, appears on all channels, with a consistent morphology, physiological cycle lengths (for example regular at around 300 ms for VT at 200 bpm) and a plausible onset. The underlying rhythm visible on the far-field EGM is the most useful argument for deciding. The pitfall is to conclude "non-sustained VT" and leave the patient exposed to a shock.
tele-069.aRetenir: Lead noise: impossible intervals, near-field only, abnormal impedance, reproducible with movement.
tele-069.rappel: Lead noise arises from non-cardiac signals picked up by the sensing circuit: conductor fracture, insulation breach, a faulty connection at the header, more rarely external interference or myopotentials. It is distinguished from a true arrhythmia by non-physiological intervals, too short for myocardial activity (the myocardium has a refractory period), confinement to the sensing channel, an associated change in impedance and reproduction by provocative manoeuvres (arm movements, pressure on the pocket). Comparison with the shock EGM, which shows the underlying rhythm, is the most useful argument.

tele-070.question: ICD: the shock circuit impedance, stable at around 50 Ω for years, is measured at over 200 Ω on the automatic daily test. What do you fear and what do you do?
options: No significance: shock impedance varies widely from one automatic test to the next
Battery at ERI: the test pulses are distorted, plan replacement
High-voltage circuit fault: shock possibly ineffective, urgent device check
T-wave oversensing: adjust sensitivity at the next device check
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): a clear, abrupt rise after years of stability is not measurement variability.
Incorrect: this parameter has nothing to do with the battery.
Correct: a "red" alert; risk of an ineffective shock during true VF, lead revision often required.
Incorrect: shock impedance has nothing to do with T-wave sensing.
tele-070.explication: The ICD regularly measures the impedance of the defibrillation circuit using very low-energy pulses. A clear, abrupt rise usually reflects a fault in the high-voltage conductor or connection, with a risk of an ineffective, or even absent, shock during true VF. It is a critical ("red") alert in the 2023 HRS consensus: the patient must be seen promptly and lead revision is often required. Depending on the coil involved, temporary reprogramming of the shock pathway may be considered. This parameter has nothing to do with the battery or with T-wave sensing.
tele-070.aRetenir: Soaring shock impedance = potentially ineffective shock: emergency.
tele-070.rappel: An ICD regularly measures shock circuit impedance using painless, very low-energy pulses; with current leads, it usually lies at a few tens of ohms, and what matters most is its stability over time. A sudden rise indicates a fault in the high-voltage conductor or connection, with a risk of an ineffective or undelivered shock during true VF. A very marked fall may, conversely, suggest a short circuit. These abnormalities do not necessarily affect pacing or sensing, which use other conductors, hence the value of automatic measurement.

tele-071.question: Dual-coil ICD (RV and SVC). An episode of VF required two shocks: the first, delivered along the RV → can + SVC pathway, was ineffective with an abnormally high measured impedance; the next one terminated the VF. For the past few days, the automatically measured shock impedance has been high, while pacing impedance and sensing are normal. What is the most appropriate course of action pending lead revision?
options: Reduce shock energy to lower the measured impedance of the shock circuit
Under monitoring, test each pathway and exclude a faulty SVC coil
No action until revision: the second shock was effective
Disable all therapies until revision, with the patient at home
commentaires: Incorrect: energy changes neither the impedance nor the conductor fault.
Correct: identify the faulty pathway and, if the fault is confined to the SVC coil, temporarily shock RV → can, then revise the lead.
Incorrect: an effective second shock guarantees nothing for subsequent ones.
Incorrect: this would leave the patient unprotected against VF.
tele-071.explication: A high shock impedance with normal pacing and sensing points to an isolated fault in the high-voltage circuit (a coil conductor or connection), for example in the SVC coil conductor, which is exposed to mechanical stress along its subclavian course. A shock delivered through a faulty circuit may be ineffective, which is potentially fatal. In hospital and under monitoring, the faulty pathway is identified by measuring the impedance of each configuration; if the fault is confined to the SVC coil, it can be excluded from the shock pathway as a temporary fix (RV to can) pending revision, bearing in mind that the efficacy of the new pathway is not guaranteed. Disabling therapies would leave the patient unprotected, and reducing energy changes neither the impedance nor the conductor fault. An effective second shock guarantees nothing for subsequent ones.
tele-071.aRetenir: Ineffective shock + high shock impedance: identify and exclude the faulty pathway, then revise the lead.
tele-071.rappel: A dual-coil ICD can deliver shocks along several pathways: RV coil to can, RV coil to SVC coil, or RV coil to can and SVC coil combined, the most common nominal configuration. Measuring the impedance of each pathway makes it possible to localise a conductor or connection fault. As a temporary fix, excluding the faulty coil from the shock circuit may restore defibrillation, with no guarantee of efficacy since the defibrillation threshold depends on the pathway. These manipulations are carried out in hospital, under monitoring, pending lead revision.

tele-072.question: Friday, 5 pm: noise alert on an ICD's RV lead, with an impedance change and numerous non-sustained VT episodes with very short intervals. The patient has not yet received a shock. Describe your management.
tele-072.reponseAttendue: Review the EGMs (non-physiological intervals, near-field only) to confirm noise. Call the patient immediately, without waiting until Monday. Refer them the same day to a centre able to interrogate and reprogram the ICD (emergency department, CCU), with instructions to call the emergency services (15 in France) if a shock occurs. On site, under monitoring: confirm the fracture or connection fault, reprogram temporarily to prevent inappropriate shocks (therapies suspended under continuous ECG monitoring, with an external defibrillator at hand), then lead revision. Document every action and inform the on-call electrophysiology team.
tele-072.explication: ICD lead noise is one of the few remote monitoring alerts that warrant immediate action: an inappropriate shock can occur at any moment, sometimes in series, and a failing lead may also fail to protect against true VF. The time of day does not change the urgency: the clinic protocol must cover this scenario (on-call rota, referral to an implanting centre). Suspending therapies is only acceptable under continuous monitoring, with an external defibrillator at hand. Lead revision resolves the problem definitively. LIA-type algorithms buy time but do not replace this course of action.
tele-072.aRetenir: ICD lead noise = same-day action, whatever the time, and therapies suspended only under monitoring.
tele-072.rappel: Suspending ICD therapies (by programming or with a magnet) exposes the patient to untreated VF: this measure is acceptable only with continuous ECG monitoring, an external defibrillator immediately available and a team able to use it, until lead revision or reactivation of therapies. The protocol of a remote monitoring centre must provide for handling critical alerts outside working hours: an on-call pathway, referral to a centre able to interrogate and reprogram the device, and instructions to the patient. Every step is documented.

tele-073.question: "ERI" (elective replacement indicator) alert on the pacemaker of a patient who is not pacemaker-dependent. What is the usual course of action?
options: No action until the end-of-life (EOL) alert is reached
Disable remote monitoring to save the remaining battery
Replace the generator urgently the same day, before it stops
Plan generator replacement within the following weeks
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): waiting for end of life leads to degraded function and then cessation of pacing.
Incorrect: remote monitoring is precisely what allows this phase to be monitored.
Incorrect (over-reaction): ERI leaves a margin of about 3 months; not urgent in a non-dependent patient.
Correct: a "yellow" alert; replacement to be scheduled, usually within 3 months.
tele-073.explication: ERI signals that the battery has reached a level at which replacement should be scheduled; the manufacturer guarantees function for a defined period (typically about 3 months) before end of life. In a non-dependent patient, it is a non-critical alert ("yellow" in the 2023 HRS consensus, unlike battery end of life, classified as "red") but should not be left to drift: generator replacement is planned. Waiting for end of life leads to degraded function and then cessation of pacing. The value of remote monitoring is precisely that it detects ERI without waiting for the annual check. The time frame should be shortened in a dependent patient or an ICD patient.
tele-073.aRetenir: ERI = replacement to be scheduled within the following weeks, sooner if pacemaker-dependent or ICD.
tele-073.rappel: The life of a device battery is marked by indicators: BOL (beginning of life), ERI (elective replacement indicator), then EOL or EOS (end of life or end of service). At ERI, the manufacturer guarantees normal or simplified operation for a defined period, allowing replacement to be scheduled; beyond that, function is no longer guaranteed. The timing of replacement takes into account the patient's dependence and the type of device (sooner for an ICD or a pacemaker-dependent patient). Longevity depends on the percentage of pacing, programmed amplitudes, impedances, delivered therapies and transmissions.

tele-074.question: What consequence may occur when a pacemaker reaches ERI?
options: Pacing rate increased to 120 bpm to signal ERI
Leads rendered unusable, to be replaced along with the generator
Switch to a simplified fallback mode, with some features disabled
Systematic switch to asynchronous DOO mode, as with a magnet
commentaires: Incorrect: at ERI, the lower rate may instead decrease, depending on the model.
Incorrect: the leads are unaffected and are usually retained.
Correct: fallback mode (often VVI), fixed rate, rate response and some diagnostics disabled, depending on the model.
Incorrect: DOO corresponds to the magnet mode of some pacemakers, not to ERI in general.
tele-074.explication: At ERI, many devices switch to simplified operation: a fallback mode (often VVI or a single-chamber mode), a fixed rate, deactivation of rate response and of some diagnostic features, and sometimes a lower base rate, depending on the manufacturer and model. The patient may experience fatigue or pacemaker syndrome. A switch to DOO corresponds to the magnet mode of some pacemakers, not to ERI in general. The leads are unaffected and are usually retained at generator replacement. The model's manual should be consulted, as behaviours vary.
tele-074.aRetenir: At ERI, the device may switch to a simplified fallback mode: replacement must be planned.
tele-074.rappel: As they approach end of life, many pacemakers reduce their consumption by simplifying their operation: switching to a single-chamber mode (often VVI), a fixed rate, disabling rate response and some diagnostic functions, sometimes a fall in the pacing rate. In most models the magnet rate also changes at ERI, which helps to identify it. These behaviours vary by manufacturer and model, hence the need to consult the manual. The patient may experience fatigue or pacemaker syndrome. At replacement, functioning leads are retained.

tele-075.question: True or false: an ERI alert on a pacemaker always requires emergency admission the same day.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: ERI leaves several weeks of margin to schedule replacement.
Correct: ERI = plan; urgency applies to end of life (EOL), dependence with malfunction or abnormally rapid depletion.
tele-075.explication: ERI leaves a margin of several weeks of operation, allowing replacement to be scheduled under good conditions. In most cases there is no same-day urgency. Urgency becomes real if the device is already at end of life (EOL/EOS), if the patient is pacemaker-dependent with deteriorating function, or if the battery is depleting abnormally fast (suspected device fault). The opposite pitfall is to forget the alert and let the battery reach end of life.
tele-075.rappel: ERI is an indicator designed to allow time to schedule generator replacement, not an emergency. The level of urgency increases in three situations: a battery already at end of life (EOL/EOS), when function is no longer guaranteed; a pacemaker-dependent patient with degraded function; and abnormally rapid battery depletion compared with the expected trend, which raises suspicion of a device fault or excess current drain (insulation breach, high outputs). Remote monitoring makes it possible to follow the battery trend and detect such deviations without waiting for the clinic visit.

tele-076.question: The platform reports that an ICD patient has not transmitted for several weeks. What should be done?
options: Remove them from the remote monitoring program after sending a letter
Call the patient to find the cause and restore the connection
Bring them in urgently for interrogation with the programmer
Wait for the next in-person visit, when the data will be reviewed
commentaires: Incorrect: removing the patient amounts to accepting a loss of opportunity.
Correct: unplugged transmitter, app disabled, travel, hospital admission… a phone call resolves most cases.
Incorrect (over-reaction): the cause is usually practical and can be fixed over the phone.
Incorrect (under-reaction): in the meantime, the patient is no longer monitored.
tele-076.explication: A disconnected patient is no longer monitored, even though both the clinic and the patient may believe otherwise. The 2023 HRS consensus emphasises active monitoring of connectivity and a protocol for managing loss of connection: calling the patient, helping with reconnection, replacing the transmitter, informing the manufacturer. The causes are often simple: transmitter unplugged or placed far from the bed, smartphone replaced, Bluetooth or app disabled, travel, hospital admission. Removing the patient from the programme or waiting for the next check amounts to accepting a loss of opportunity.
tele-076.aRetenir: Loss of transmission = unmonitored patient: call and reconnect.
tele-076.rappel: Connectivity monitoring is an integral part of remote monitoring: the platform flags patients who have not transmitted beyond a defined period, and the centre's protocol specifies who contacts them and within what time frame. A disconnected patient is no longer monitored, often without the patient or the team being aware of it. Most causes are practical and are resolved by telephone; the others require replacement of the transmitter or contact with the manufacturer. The proportion of connected patients is a quality indicator for the centre.

tele-077.question: What are common causes of missing transmissions in remote monitoring?
options: Transmitter unplugged or away from the bedroom
Smartphone app uninstalled or Bluetooth switched off
Prolonged stay away from home
Device battery still far from ERI
Change of phone without re-pairing
commentaires: Correct: this is the most common cause.
Correct: common with smartphone-connected devices.
Correct: travel or hospital admission takes the patient away from the transmitter.
Incorrect: a battery far from ERI obviously does not explain missing transmissions.
Correct: without re-pairing, the app no longer transmits.
tele-077.explication: Loss of connectivity is usually due to practical issues: transmitter unplugged, moved or far from the bed, patient travelling or in hospital and, for smartphone-connected devices, app uninstalled, Bluetooth switched off, battery-saving restrictions or a change of phone without re-pairing. A battery still far from ERI obviously does not explain missing transmissions. Patient education at enrolment and active monitoring of connectivity reduce these losses. Every clinic must specify who calls, and within what time frame.
tele-077.aRetenir: Most losses of transmission have a practical cause that a phone call can fix.
tele-077.rappel: Transmission relies either on a bedside transmitter at home, which must stay plugged in and close to the patient during sleep, or on a smartphone app communicating with the device via Bluetooth Low Energy. Each link can break the connection: an unplugged or moved transmitter, no network, travel or hospital admission, and with smartphones, a closed or uninstalled app, Bluetooth switched off, battery-saving settings, an operating system update or a change of phone without re-pairing. Patient education and active connectivity monitoring limit these interruptions.

tele-078.question: Implantable loop recorder for syncope: "5 s pause" alert. On the EGM, the QRS complexes gradually become very low in amplitude and are no longer counted, while small regular complexes remain visible throughout the "pause". What is your interpretation?
options: Paroxysmal AV block: arrange pacemaker implantation very promptly
Vagal sinus pause: postural advice and simple follow-up
False pause (undersensing): no pacemaker, adjust sensing
True 5 s asystole: urgent indication for a pacemaker
commentaires: Incorrect: AV block would show non-conducted P waves on an isoelectric baseline, not regular complexes.
Incorrect: a true sinus pause would show an isoelectric line.
Correct: regular complexes visible during the "pause" indicate undersensing of low-amplitude QRS complexes.
Incorrect: this is not asystole; implanting a pacemaker on the basis of this tracing would be a mistake.
tele-078.explication: False pauses are common on implantable loop recorders: when QRS amplitude falls (posture, movement, poor electrode contact), the complexes drop below the sensing threshold and the device wrongly concludes that there is a pause. Regular complexes visible during the "pause" indicate undersensing. A pacemaker must certainly not be indicated on the basis of this type of episode. Sensitivity or sensing filters can be adjusted, and EGMs should always be reviewed. A true pause shows an isoelectric line, possibly with non-conducted P waves in AV block.
tele-078.aRetenir: Complexes visible during a "pause" = undersensing, not asystole.
tele-078.rappel: An implantable loop recorder detects QRS complexes on a low-amplitude subcutaneous signal recorded between two closely spaced electrodes, and triggers a recording when no QRS is sensed for a programmed duration (pause) or when the rate rises above or falls below set limits. Signal amplitude varies with posture, movement and device contact, leading to undersensing. A true pause is recognised by an isoelectric line, possibly with non-conducted P waves in AV block. Any indication for pacing rests on a reviewed EGM, ideally correlated with symptoms.

tele-079.question: Implantable loop recorder: very frequent "AF" alerts in a patient in sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions. The EGMs show P waves before each QRS and irregular RR intervals due to the PACs. What should be done?
options: Anticoagulate the patient, as the episodes are numerous and recurrent
Disable all of the loop recorder's alerts to relieve the team
Explant the loop recorder, now a source of repeated false alerts
Label them false positives and tune AF detection, keeping alerts on
commentaires: Incorrect: P waves before each QRS rule out AF; anticoagulation would be a serious error.
Incorrect: the purpose of the device would be lost.
Incorrect: explantation is not justified; reprogramming is sufficient.
Correct: review, classify, adjust sensitivity and minimum duration, while keeping the relevant alerts.
